title: Teaching Information
text:
I am a strong believer that any student can learn from the right teacher. I have had many, many conversations with students whose biggest struggle often comes down to a disconnect between the teacher (or professor) and the student. The relationship between students and teachers often times reminds me of Plato’s The Cave. The teacher is trying to introduce the student to the teacher’s world, but the student is viewing the teacher’s world through the lens of the student’s own understanding of the world. Each step is a breach into the student’s understanding of the world, and the wrong guide may struggle to help them. Additionally, my experience in teaching has taught me that the teacher is also only capable of interpreting the world from their own perspective, and the student is also attempting to introduce the teacher into the student’s view of the world. Perhaps that is just an analogy for communication in general, but it resonates with me as an apt way to describe the difficulty in being both the teacher and the student. Both are captives to their own perspectives.
We cannot meet the needs of every student, and we cannot force every student to put in effort, but we can make a difference.

title: Choosing a Programming Language
text:
Python is my language of choice. In my opinion, choosing a language to start learning how to operate in is much less important than simply starting to learn. Going between different programming languages requires learning new words, sure, but the logic behind how computers handle information does not vary wildly. The logic behind computer science is essentially a form of math, and logical concepts such as multiplication and addition both work just fine even if we change bases or how we represent them.
Example:
Python makes a lot of assumptions for you. If you want to store a number to use later, you simply tell it: x = 5, and it will run that no problem. Python sees a whole number on its own and assumes that it is an integer1. It handles the memory and background categorization for you.
C does not make the same assumptions that Python does. If you put x = 5 into C, it will break. C assumes nothing about what x is supposed to be, so it doesn’t know how much memory to give it. You need to explicitly tell it that x is an integer by writing int x = 5;, and it will handle it no problem.
The logic of storing and manipulating data is a simple process, but the language used to describe it changes. Learning the logic of computers is often the hardest part for people, and transitioning to another language after that is not nearly as difficult. That being said, choosing a language to begin with often goes hand-in-hand with what you want to accomplish.



Python
+ Industry standard for AI, machine learning, and data science
+ Excellent data handling/analysis ability (uses packages that run highly optimized C/Fortran code in the background)
+ Very beginner-friendly
+ Makes lots of assumptions (handles memory for you)
+ Tons of useful packages created by others
- Slow execution speed
- Whitespace matters
- Can hide the inner workings, making performance issues harder to debug
- Makes lots of assumptions (less manual control) 


C or C++
+ Unmatched processing speed and precise memory control
+ Can run on pretty much every piece of hardware
+ Industry standard for systems programming and hardware integration
+ C++ in particular is the standard for game development (Unreal Engine)
- Complex syntax
- Need to understand manual memory handling
- Assumes very little (you have to build everything explicitly) 


Fortran
+ Extremely fast and efficient for heavy numerical arrays and complex math
+ Tons of use in scientific computing and supercomputing
+ Can explicitly manage memory handling
+ Decades and decades of optimized math libraries to pull from 
- Super old
- Need to explicitly understand memory handling
- Not suited for general-purpose programming or modern UX 


Java and C#
+ Industry standards for massive corporate application development
+ Highly general-purpose (they power everything from mobile apps to heavy enterprise servers)
+ Object-oriented, making them scalable for large teams
+ C# for game development (Unity) 
- Syntax is verbose (requires a lot of boilerplate code)
- Can have slower startup times and higher memory overhead than C/C++ 


Javascript / Typescript
+ Industry standard for web development
+ Runs natively in web browsers
+ Full-stack development possible (one language for front-end and back-end)
+ Massive industry and community
+ TypeScript adds strict rules (types) to prevent messy errors in large projects
- Large, complex dependency trees
- Vanilla JavaScript can be prone to runtime errors 


Rust and Go
+ Industry standard for Web3, microservices, and modern cloud infrastructure
+ Rust can be extremely fast (comparable to C) and guarantees memory safety
+ Go is designed to be easy to learn and handles thousands of simultaneous tasks effortlessly 
- Rust is notoriously difficult to learn
- Go syntax is extremely verbose (requires writing repetitive code because it lacks certain advanced features) 



Do you want to work in data analysis or AI? Choose Python. Do you want to work in game development? Choose either C++ or C#. Do you want to delve into the ins and outs of how a computer handles information? Choose C. Do you want to be able to hang with all of the old computational physicists and complain about how slow Python is? Choose Fortran. Do you want to become a full-stack or web developer? Choose Javascript/Typescript. Do you want to make a phone app? Choose Java. Rust and Go are so new that I honestly don’t know much about them, but if you want to dive into those new territories, go for it!
If you don’t know what you want to do yet, then I’ll make it simple for you. Just start with Python.

title: What is a Programming Language?
text:
Think of writing code as providing an explicit set of instructions to a computer. The programming language is an interpreter that takes the code and translates it into something that the computer can understand. A programming language, in many ways, is exactly that—a language. It has its own syntax, grammar, and vocabulary.
Let’s say you speak English, but you want to communicate with someone who speaks Chinese. In order to communicate, there needs to be some way for the two of you to understand each other. One possibility is for you to simply learn Chinese so well that you can communicate whatever you need to. This kind of approach can take a very long time and requires quite a bit of study. To talk to a computer like this, instead of learning Chinese, you would essentially be learning how to flip bits on and off and speak in binary. Binary has its own structure that is very different from most spoken and written languages and can provide an even greater challenge to learn.
Instead of learning Chinese to communicate, you can find someone who already speaks Chinese and ask them to translate for you. The problem is, this translator doesn’t understand English perfectly; they understand it in a way that is very literal and basic. The translator also has no mind of their own to read between the lines or understand connotations or implications. In order to communicate, you need to be very exact with the words you choose to say to the translator.
It might be helpful to think of a programming language as a child that is only capable of doing things that you teach it to do. Want it to know what a banana is? You need to TEACH it what a banana is. Want it to understand how to write its name? You need to TEACH it to write its name. Want it to solve a complicated problem? You need to TEACH it HOW to solve the problem. The advantage of languages like Python is that other people have often figured out how to teach the language to do some very useful things, and you can utilize what other people have done. I’m not going to spend my time telling the code, in its language, how to compute a logarithm; I’m simply going to import the NumPy package because somebody else has already done that.
Let’s see how it might work telling this computer translator to “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.”
The translator will attempt to recognize each word because it can only translate literally:
The translator breaks. It doesn’t know what to do because it does not know what a “sandwich” is. If programmed properly, the translator will throw an error: “Error: I don’t know what ‘sandwich’ is.” This is the translator’s way of saying: “If you want your statement translated, you need to explicitly define what a ‘sandwich’ is first.”
Now, we have to figure out a way to define a sandwich in terms the translator can understand. We can try telling it something like: “‘sandwich’ = food between 2 slices of bread”.
The translator will now attempt to process this new definition:
Now you can attempt to run the original statement again: “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich”
Python, C++, Fortran, etc., are all simply translators. They each have their own specific syntax and rules connected to very specific computer translations. You can only work within the framework of these computer/human translations.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text: The term bit is short for binary digit. It is a system that has two states: 0 or 1, hence the “bi-” in binary. If you are particularly inquisitive, you may ask “Why 0 or 1?” The answer is that it doesn’t really matter which two numbers we choose, any two will do. The point is that we stay consistent. For example, I have made circuits that look for two inputs: 0V or 5V. That is still a binary system. The reason we represent bits as 0 or 1 is because of simplicity.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
How are 0 and 1 Simple?
The number 0 is often associated with “nothing” or “off” in many people’s daily lives. 1 is clearly “not zero” or “not nothing” or “something.” If I asked you “Is there a dog in your room?” and your answer was “no” then that would correspond to 0 dogs in your room. If your answer was instead “yes” then that would correspond to at least 1 dog being there. By this logic, the number 0 essentially represents the absence of something and the number 1 represents the presence of something. This is at the heart of the simplicity of the bit.
That logic also provides the answer to another question that you might have. Why does it have to be binary? Why not trinary (0,1,2)? or quaternary (0,1,2,3)? Or any other number of -nary in existence? Again, simplicity is the answer. The simplest way I can think of representing something is asking does it exist or not? No other details, just the very basic question does it exist or not? Is there a dog in your room? The answer is either no (0) or yes (1). There is little room for confusion or complications because the question and the answer are both extremely simple. This simplicity is extremely important, especially when we want to build more complicated structures out of it.

title: The Basics
text:
So, we now know what a bit is from a technical perspective and some logic about why it makes sense, but what is a bit really? This is the truly fascinating part of the underlying science behind computers. A bit is actually a single unit of information. There is an entire field of science called Information Theory that has been in development for around 160 years and seen massive strides in the past 100 years. In fact, the accelerating advancements in technology that we have seen since around WWII have been parallel to accelerating advancements in Information Theory. Some of you have likely heard of quantum computers that rely on qubits but may not realize that qubits are a direct succession of the bit in Quantum Information Theory.
I will provide more of the logic of information theory that led to bits, modern computers, and qubits, but the gist of it is that in 1867 a famous physicist named James Clerk Maxwell was trying to find a way to poke holes in the second law of thermodynamics (entropy always increases in a closed system). His thought experiment, called Maxwell’s Demon, is still somewhat relevant to this day. It has been solved, probably. But it still persists nonetheless. This thought experiment eventually led to the discovery that information is a real, physical quantity. Just like you measure your height in feet, inches, and centimeters, information is measured in bits.
For those curious about how it is possible that information is a physical quantity, I recommend reading my section on the development of Information Theory. It is not comprehensive, but it provides a thought path to arrive at the conclusions that we are at today.
One of the reasons that I like to point out all of this is that now we can finally, truly understand why computers function on bits. Think about it this way, in order to exchange information, you need a way to represent the information. Picture someone using a flashlight to transmit messages in morse code. The photons coming from the flashlight do not have some special property that allows them to carry information, and yet an exchange of information is able to happen because we are able to encode information into the existence and nonexistence of photons from the flashlight.
An elusive piece of the puzzle here is the idea that information is tied to units of energy in a relationship with negative entropy. While that may sound complicated because entropy is a fancy word coopted by sci-fi media to be very mysterious, it has a relatively simple idea that you can use here. Entropy refers to the disorder of a system. In essence, it is a measure of how likely the state of a system is to occur. If I do 30 cap flips with water bottles, the likelihood that every water bottle lands perfectly on its cap is very small. An arrangement of 30 water bottles placed perfectly on their caps is a very low entropy system, because it is highly unlikely to find this in nature. On the other hand, an arrangement of 30 water bottles strewn about randomly is a much higher entropy system because it is much more likely to be found in nature. In order to go from the random system to the ordered system, it takes a certain amount of energy. Information is associated with the dissolution of chaos, the destruction of disorder. In other words, information relies on the ability to reduce the entropy of a system. In the following flashlight example, the flashing of the light in a very specific pattern is associated with a certain amount of entropy. If the flashlight were purely flashing determined by its most likely state, there would be no information associated with it. But, giving flashes of the flashlight a specific order to encode information reduces the entropy of the flashing light. This is why information is often referred to as a type of negative entropy.
Let’s represent the flashlight being off as 0 and the flashlight being on as 1. We will go with simplest possible case and make a single bit equal to a single unit of morse code. Here is how a message might look1:
010100000001011101010001110111011100010101011100010000000111010111000101110001011101000101110001110111011100011101011100010
This translates to “I love karoake”. I started and ended the message with a 0 to take into account the information associated with not having a signal at the beginning and end. Sending that message in this manner took 123 bits. Does this mean that the information that I, personally, love karaoke has a physical size of 123 bits? No, not really. The message itself is not the same as the human concepts of love or karaoke. It merely
Why does all of this matter? Let’s start building simple systems.
A light switch has 2 positions: off (0) and on (1).
If the light is on, you dance. If the light is off, you don’t dance.
I flip the switch to on (1). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance
I flip the switch to off (0). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
Now, I’m going to put something in there to mess with the signal from the switch. When the switch is on (1), the light is off (0). When the switch is off (0), the light is on (1). This is likely a familiar situation to many people that have rooms with multiple light switches controlling the same lights.
I flip the switch to on (1). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
I flip the switch to off (0). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance.
Messing with a signal like this is called a gate. This example of changing 0 to 1 and 1 to 0 is called a NOT gate. It is a simple logical play on a bit. You do the opposite of what a bit does. If you think about this from an electricity standpoint it makes sense to wonder how no signal, meaning no electricity, can possibly activate the light in the NOT situation (because 0 sends 1). In situations like this, there is a source of electricity that allows the gate to pass along a signal when it receives no signal from the circuit, so try not to get hung up on that idea.
Let’s try building some more logic. We are now going to use 2 switches, or 2 bits. To mess with it this time, I am going to make it so that the lights turn on only when BOTH switches are on (1,1).
Both switches are off (0,0). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
The left switch is on and the other is off (1,0). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
The right switch is on and the other is off (0,1). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
Both switches are on (1,1). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance.
This type of gate is called an AND gate. It only outputs a 1 if it receives a 1,1 input.
There are a multitude of gates that can be used in physical circuits and in logic. Complicated combinations of these gates in physical circuits give us the ability to create modern technology such as computers. These logical sequences of information theory are the exact same tenets that created programming languages. Your computer “thinks” and functions by utilizing bits and gates. Programming languages were devised as a way manipulate bits and gates to make computers do things.
This is why I think that it is important for anyone diving into the subject of programming to understand a little bit about the basics of information theory and computers, because programming languages can seem like a mystical thing that doesn’t make sense. It is quite the opposite, they are very purposeful and follow rigid, logical systems.
An extension of this that is very relevant is to go back to the idea that information is a physical quantity and think about this idea of a bit being 0 or 1. What if there was a way that you could actually store whether a switch was was on or off? In the flashlight morse code example, each subsequent bit erases the state of the previous. But, let’s say that we have 123 physical switches that use up to correspond to 1 and off to correspond to 0. We could set these physical switches in the positions of that message, then leave it there and go do something else. When we come back, the bits are still in the same position that we left them. This ability to store information, rather than merely transmit it, is called memory.
Memory hardware has advanced significantly in the last 30 years. In order to store information, even temporarily, you need to have a physical way to contain it just like having physical switches. This is one of the physical limitations of modern computers and is exactly why you cannot just download more RAM. Random Access Memory (RAM) is very fast memory designed to hold things temporarily. Hard Disk Drives (HDD) which are quickly becoming obsolete use a metal disk and a little magnet to literally write information (bits) to the metal disk. Solid State Drives (SSD) are much faster than HDDs because they do not use a spinning disk. I do not recall the specific mechanism, but given the name I assume they manipulate the electron structure of metals (mess with the crystal pattern of the electrons).
Anything you do on your computer uses memory. RAM will be the primary limiting component for programming because it is the quick-access memory that programs are using. There is also a limitation for how fast a Central Processing Unit (CPU) or Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is able to move the information around, but that is not usually a massive roadblock to people.


The CPU is typically very fast at singular tasks. CPUs do a great job at handling tasks that have large sequential components. Maybe you write a program teaching the computer to do a kickflip. In order to do a kickflip it has to first learn what a kickflip is, then what a skateboard is, then learn to ride a skateboard, then learn to do an ollie, then learn to do a kickflip, then actually do a kickflip. CPUs are very fast at getting through steps like this. They are not so fast at doing multiple things at once. If you knew exactly how to paint every part of a picture, a CPU would still need to go paint every individual part of the painting spot-by-spot using 1 paintbrush. This is where a GPU is useful instead. GPUs are slower at doing 1 thing, but they can do many things at once. If you know exactly how to paint a picture, the GPU will simply use 50 paintbrushes to paint it all at once. This is a much, much faster process than painting spot-by-spot using 1 paintbrush like the CPU. That being said, the GPU is much, much slower at learning to do a kickflip because it still needs to learn all of the things first before actually doing to kickflip.

text:
What is a Bit Really Though?
Calling a bit a binary digit or a system with 2 states doesn’t actually tell us what a bit is. This is the truly fascinating part of the underlying science behind computers. A bit is actually a single unit of information. There is an entire field of science called Information Theory that has been in development for around 160 years and seen massive strides in the past 100 years. In fact, the accelerating advancements in technology that we have seen since around WWII have been parallel to accelerating advancements in Information Theory. Some of you have likely heard of quantum computers that rely on qubits but may not realize that qubits are simply a quantum version of bits used in Quantum Information Theory.
Without going into a full history of Information Theory, the gist of it is that in 1867 a famous physicist named James Clerk Maxwell was trying to find a way to poke holes in the second law of thermodynamics (entropy always increases in a closed system) and came up with a logic test for it. His thought experiment, called Maxwell’s Demon, is still somewhat relevant to this day. It has been solved, probably. But it still persists in some ways. The pursuit of resolving Maxwell’s Demon eventually led to the realization that information is a real, physical quantity. title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Representing Information with Bits
In order to exchange or store information, we need a way to represent the information. Picture someone using a flashlight to transmit messages in morse code. The photons coming from the flashlight do not have some special property that allows them to carry information, and yet an exchange of information is able to happen because we are able to encode information into the existence and nonexistence of photons from the flashlight. To go another level deeper, the encoding is actually tied to the alteration of the entropy1 of the flashlight.
Let’s represent the flashlight being off as 0 and the flashlight being on as 1. We will go with simplest possible case and make a single bit equal to a single unit of morse code. Here is how a message might look2:
010100000001011101010001110111011100010101011100010000000111010111000101110001011101000101110001110111011100011101011100010
This translates to “I love karoake”. I started and ended the message with a 0 to take into account the information associated with not having a signal at the beginning and end. Sending that message in this manner took 123 bits. Does this mean that the information that I, personally, love karaoke has a physical size of 123 bits? No, not really. The message “I love karaoke” is what we encoded in 123 bits, not the information of what any of that means. In fact, it is important here to separate your colloquial definition of information about the meaning of something from the scientific definition of information.
The 123 bits that I chose to use to transmit this message could easily have been done with 121 bits by leaving out the bordering 0’s. It could have been represented with 200 bits if I decided to add more bordering 0’s or maybe use a different system of representation altogether. Morse himself designed Morse Code to utilize less time spent on more common letters, so common letters are more typically composed of dots. Dots have a bit size of 1 while dashes have a bit size of 3. What if I change around the Morse system and now my message might take 500 bits to send, or 50 bits?
The bits measuring information don’t hold some grandiose, obscure meaning in them. The information is contained in specifically ordering the bits in the way that we choose. If I send the word “love” to 100 people, it may mean 100 different things to all of those people. The information contained by the bits is not the meaning of the word love, but specifically is just the word love.

There is also a limitation for how fast a Central Processing Unit (CPU) or Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is able to move the information around, but that is not usually a massive roadblock to people.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Information is Negative Entropy
In the early days of resolving Maxwell’s Demon, Leo Szilard developed the idea that knowledge is associated with a dissolution of entropy. Knowledge, and information, become intrinsically related to the energy associated with reducing the entropy in a system.
Entropy is a measure of the order or disorder of a system. One way to think of entropy is how likely a system is to exist by pure randomness. If we flip 30 bottles and 30 land perfectly on their caps upside down (a cap flip), that final 30 bottle system is a very low entropy system. If instead only a few or none land perfectly on their caps upside down, which is far more likely, then it is a high entropy system. More naturally-random results = more entropy. An interesting point is that you can very specifically arrange the 30 bottles as if they had all been perfectly cap-flipped, and this final system of 30 water bottles will have the same state as very low entropy state of them all having randomly landed on their caps. There is an energy associated with taking the bottles from a high entropy state (more likely to exist) to a low entropy state (less likely to exist).
The information contained by a flashing flashlight actually arises from specifically arranging the flashes of the flashlight in such a way. It is not even really the bits themselves that contain the information, but rather the change in entropy of the state in which you arrange the bits away from their likely (more random) state. Storing or communicating information explicitly require setting a system into a lower entropy state, and it is this state that contains the information. The bits are just a way to represent this state.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
What is a Bit?
The term bit is short for binary digit . It is a system that exists in one of two states: 0 or 1, which gives us the “bi-” in binary .
If you are inquisitive, you might ask, “Why exactly 0 and 1?” The truth is, the specific numbers don’t matter as long as we choose exactly two states and stay consistent . For example, physical computer circuits look for two voltage inputs: 0V or 5V . That is still a binary system. We represent bits as 0 or 1 purely for mathematical simplicity .

The Simplicity of 0 and 1
In daily life, the number 0 is often associated with “nothing” or “off.” By contrast, 1 is clearly “not zero,” representing “something” or “on” .
If I asked you, “Is there a dog in your room?” and your answer was “no”, that corresponds to 0 dogs . If your answer was “yes”, that corresponds to at least 1 dog . By this logic, 0 represents the absence of something, and 1 represents the presence of something . This is the heart of a bit’s simplicity .
Why does it have to be binary? Why not ternary (0, 1, 2) or quaternary (0, 1, 2, 3)?  The simplest way to evaluate reality is to ask a fundamental question: Does this exist, or not?  There is little room for confusion because both the question and the answer are absolute . This absolute simplicity is vital when we want to stack millions of these questions together to build complex computational structures .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
What is a Bit, Really?
Calling a bit a “binary digit” doesn’t actually explain its physical nature . A bit is actually a single unit of information .
There is an entire field of science called Information Theory that has been evolving for over 160 years . The accelerating technological advancements we have seen since WWII run parallel to breakthroughs in this field . (If you have heard of quantum computers, they rely on qubits, which are simply the quantum mechanical version of bits used in Quantum Information Theory ).
In 1867, a famous physicist named James Clerk Maxwell proposed a thought experiment—known as Maxwell’s Demon—to test the second law of thermodynamics . The pursuit of resolving this physics puzzle eventually led scientists to a profound realization: Information is a real, physical quantity . Just as you measure distance in meters, you measure information in bits .

Representing Information
To exchange or store information, we must encode it into a physical medium .
Picture someone using a flashlight to transmit messages in Morse code . The photons coming from the flashlight do not inherently possess special properties that carry data . Yet, communication happens because we encode information into the existence (1) and nonexistence (0) of those photons .
Let’s make a single bit equal to a single unit of Morse code time. Here is how a message might look:

010100000001011101010001110111011100010101011100010000000111010111000101110001011101000101110001110111011100011101011100010

This sequence translates to “I love karaoke” . Sending that specific pattern required 123 bits .
Does this mean the literal concept of loving karaoke has a physical mass of 123 bits? No . The bits do not hold semantic meaning; they only hold the structure of the message . If I send the word “love” to 100 people, it means 100 different things. The scientific information contained in those bits is just the structural arrangement of the word itself, not human emotion .


Information and Entropy
In the early 20th century, physicist Leo Szilard helped resolve Maxwell’s Demon by proving that acquiring information inherently requires an expenditure of energy to reduce the entropy of a system .
Entropy is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system . Think of flipping 30 water bottles. If all 30 land perfectly upside down on their caps, that is a highly ordered, very low entropy system . If they land randomly scattered, that is a highly disordered, high entropy system (which is statistically far more likely) .
Because the scattered bottles are the natural, likely state, it requires physical energy to organize them into the unlikely state of standing on their caps .
The information contained in our flashlight signal arises from intentionally arranging the flashes against random chance . Storing or communicating information explicitly requires forcing a system into a lower entropy state. The bits are simply the mathematical way we measure and represent that ordered state .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Introduction to Logic Gates
Why does the physics of information matter for programming? Because it allows us to build logic .
Imagine a simple light switch with two positions: Off (0) and On (1) . We establish a rule: If the light is on, you dance. If it is off, you do not dance .

Input 1 (Switch On): Light is on. You dance. 
Input 0 (Switch Off): Light is off. You do not dance. 

Now, we introduce a hardware component that intercepts and reverses the electrical signal. When the switch is On (1), it forces the light Off (0).

Input 1 (Switch On): Light is forced Off. You do not dance. 
Input 0 (Switch Off): Light is forced On. You dance. 

This type of signal manipulation is called a Gate . Specifically, this is a NOT Gate because it outputs the exact opposite of its input .
Let’s try a more complex logical rule using two switches. We construct the circuit so the light only turns on if BOTH switches are flipped On (1, 1) .

0, 0 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
1, 0 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
0, 1 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
1, 1 \(\rightarrow\) Light On (Dance!) 

This is an AND Gate .
By combining millions of physical NOT, AND, and OR gates on a silicon chip, we create modern computers . Programming languages were invented simply as a human-readable way to manipulate these logic gates . Code isn’t magic; it is a rigid, physical system of organized logic .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Memory and Processing
If information is a physical quantity, how do we store it? In our flashlight example, the information vanished the moment the light turned off .
To store information permanently, you need a physical container to hold the system in its low-entropy state so you can leave and come back to it later . This is called memory .

RAM (Random Access Memory): Very fast, temporary memory used by your computer to hold the data it is actively thinking about. When power is lost, the data is lost .
HDD (Hard Disk Drive): Older, slower storage that uses a magnetic arm to literally write bits onto a spinning metal platter .
SSD (Solid State Drive): Fast, modern storage with no moving parts . Instead of magnets, it relies on microscopic components called floating-gate transistors to physically trap electrons in a specific pattern, holding onto the data even when the computer is turned off.


CPU vs. GPU
To execute the logic gates and move this memory around, computers rely on processors .
The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is incredibly fast at doing single tasks in a sequential order . If you want to teach a computer to do a kickflip, the CPU learns step-by-step: first what a skateboard is, then how to ride it, then how to ollie, and finally how to kickflip . If it were painting a picture, the CPU is one master artist painting the entire canvas at lightning speed with a single brush .
The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is slower at single tasks, but excels at parallel processing—doing thousands of calculations at the exact same time . If the GPU were painting the same picture, it is like 5,000 artists painting one dot simultaneously . The GPU is much faster at rendering the final image, but it relies on the CPU to tell it what picture it is supposed to be painting in the first place.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Intro to Logic Gates
Why does all of this matter? Let’s start building simple systems.
A light switch has 2 positions: off (0) and on (1).
If the light is on, you dance. If the light is off, you don’t dance.
I flip the switch to on (1). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance
I flip the switch to off (0). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
Now, I’m going to put something in there to mess with the signal from the switch. When the switch is on (1), the light is off (0). When the switch is off (0), the light is on (1). This is likely a familiar situation to many people that have rooms with multiple light switches controlling the same lights.
I flip the switch to on (1). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
I flip the switch to off (0). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance.
Messing with a signal like this is called a gate. This example of changing 0 to 1 and 1 to 0 is called a NOT gate. It is a simple logical play on a bit. You do the opposite of what a bit does. If you think about this from an electricity standpoint it makes sense to wonder how no signal, meaning no electricity, can possibly activate the light in the NOT situation (because 0 sends 1). In situations like this, there is a source of electricity that allows the gate to pass along a signal when it receives no signal from the circuit, so try not to get hung up on that idea.
Let’s try building some more logic. We are now going to use 2 switches, or 2 bits. To mess with it this time, I am going to make it so that the lights turn on only when BOTH switches are on (1,1).

The left switch is on and the other is off (1,0). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
The right switch is on and the other is off (0,1). You see the lights off (0). What do you do?
- The answer is not dance.
Both switches are on (1,1). You see the lights on (1). What do you do?
- The answer is dance.

Complicated combinations of these gates in physical circuits give us the ability to create modern technology such as computers. These logical sequences of information theory are the exact same tenets that created programming languages. Your computer “thinks” and functions by utilizing bits and gates. Programming languages were devised as a way manipulate bits and gates to make computers do things.
This is why I think that it is important for anyone diving into the subject of programming to understand a little bit about the basics of information theory and computers, because programming languages can seem like a mystical thing that doesn’t make sense. It is quite the opposite, they are very purposeful and follow rigid, logical systems.

Memory and Processing
If information is a physical quantity, how do we store it? In our flashlight example, the information vanished the moment the light turned off .
To store information permanently, you need a physical container to hold the system in its low-entropy state so you can leave and come back to it later . This is called memory .

RAM (Random Access Memory): Very fast, temporary memory used by your computer to hold the data it is actively thinking about. When power is lost, the data is lost .
HDD (Hard Disk Drive): Older, slower storage that uses a magnetic arm to literally write bits onto a spinning metal platter .
SSD (Solid State Drive): Fast, modern storage with no moving parts . Instead of magnets, it relies on microscopic components called floating-gate transistors to physically trap electrons in a specific pattern, holding onto the data even when the computer is turned off.


CPU vs. GPU
To execute the logic gates and move this memory around, computers rely on processors .
The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is incredibly fast at doing single tasks in a sequential order . If you want to teach a computer to do a kickflip, the CPU learns step-by-step: first what a skateboard is, then how to ride it, then how to ollie, and finally how to kickflip . If it were painting a picture, the CPU is one master artist painting the entire canvas at lightning speed with a single brush .
The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is slower at single tasks, but excels at parallel processing—doing thousands of calculations at the exact same time . If the GPU were painting the same picture, it is like 5,000 artists painting one dot simultaneously . The GPU is much faster at rendering the final image, but it relies on the CPU to tell it what picture it is supposed to be painting in the first place.
